rv.q: Watching Nadia Fall’s enjoyable production, I was struck by a startling realisation about the agency, or lack thereof, afforded to all three female characters, in financial, sexual, emotional and professional spheres.
Glorious, ghastly, and very funny, Abigail's Party is still a great invite.
Revitalised by a crack cast, this is a party you won’t want to miss.

Nadia Fall’s astringent staging retains the period setting, rolling the whole thing out on Peter McKintosh’s gloriously strident set and lacing it with 1970s music, but it also drives home the current resonances.
In a diaphanous orange frock and ratted Farrah Fawcett wig, inserting one cigarette after another into her raptor’s rictus grin, Outhwaite gives a monstrous, physically precise tour de force.
Fall’s production, first seen at Stratford East in 2024, is so deftly crafted that the best of the dialogue sounds freshly minted.
Outhwaite seizes and stomps her way through it with glittering conviction.
Nadia Fall’s production taps into a ferocious, proto-feminist defiance led by Outhwaite.
Her performance, and Fall’s production as a whole, proves that this period comedy of manners is eternally resonant.
Fall’s production, though, favours a consistent tone of brash silliness over psychological intensity.
Tamzin Outhwaite dazzles demonically in this pitch-perfect revival of Mike Leigh’s acid comedy of 1970s class envy and aspiration, Abigail’s Party.
This vibrant and perfectly-pitched production means you just can't take your eyes off it.
Here, we are gifted a memorable revival that refuses to shy away from the biting social commentary of the original, while basking in its delightfully dark comedy.
Nadia Fall has directed an hilarious revival of a much-loved classic which stays true to the original whilst breathing fresh life into one of the most monstrous central characters ever written.
Fall’s revival revels in its sheer entertainment factor, emphasised by Peter McKintosh’s sitcom-esque living room set, and in Outhwaite has a comic lead on stellar form.
Fall’s Abigail’s Party is a hilarious comedy with edge, breathing life into the well-known piece.
Luckily these excesses don’t last long enough to impair the joy and hilarity of the script.
Fall’s production is broadly sympathetic and solidly performed, if a little “light”.
If you like your comedy to be raucous, this is the show for you.
A production as refreshing as putting ice and a slice of lemon in your drink, everyone involved have really come through to create a West End party you would be mad to miss.
Nevertheless, this is a fantastic version of a classic piece and a tremendously fun night out.
It pushes the pleasantries of the decade to breaking point, and makes for an entertaining night at the theatre.
Do go to this excellent show but on a settled, reasonably full stomach with a few carbs.
Yet none of this prevents the evening from being a toe-curlingly compelling watch.
Nadia Fall’s production opens up that dark underbelly of pain and is a dramatic triumph.

Its exploration of the significance of the unsaid within "polite society" and humorous critiques of the suburban "bourgeois" make for a timeless show that will both disturb and prompt laughter out loud.
But slow-moving story aside, it’s impossible to imagine a more seamless version of what is a piece of classic British theatre.

cn.t: Outhwaite triumphs in this crowd-pleasing revival of Leigh's 1970s satire, successfully escaping Steadman's shadow with a ferocious, commanding performance. Critics praise the pitch-perfect production's enduring humor, though some find it lacks venom.
